A Combined Fertility and Developmental Toxicity Study of ISIS 721744 in Mice Via
Subcutaneous Administration (Study Nos. 727-134; 721744-AS06)
Key Study Findings


Mice were treated by SC administration with vehicle control (0.9% sodium chloride for
injection), donidalorsen (1, 4, or 10 mg/kg/week), or mouse surrogate ISIS 722059
(4 mg/kg/week). Males were dosed once weekly during the premating (beginning 28 days
prior to mating), mating, and postmating phases (10 weeks total). Females were dosed
beginning 14 days prior to mating. Females were dosed weekly (Days 1, 8, 15, and 22, as
needed) during the premating phase and through the mating phase until positive evidence of
copulation was observed, and every other day during the gestation period from Gestation Day
(GD) 0 to GD 16 (i.e., GDs 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, and 16). Unmated females continued to
be dosed weekly until termination (following the last GD 18 necropsies).



There were no estrous cycle changes (i.e., mean number of cycles and mean cycle length)
related to treatment with donidalorsen or mouse surrogate ISIS 722059.



Percent abnormal sperm was increased at 10 mg/kg/week donidalorsen (15.6%, statistically
significant) and 4 mg/kg/week ISIS 722059 (13.4%), compared to the vehicle control
(10.1%), and outside of the conducting laboratory historical control ranges of 3.4% to 10.2%.
It did not appear that an increase in percent abnormal sperm affected pregnancy indices at
10 mg/kg/week donidalorsen or 4 mg/kg/week ISIS 722059.



There were no effects of donidalorsen or mouse surrogate ISIS 722059 on male or female
mating performance; the number of corpora lutea, implantations, preimplantation and
postimplantation losses, or live fetuses; fetal body weights; or fetal external, visceral, or
skeletal variations or malformations (i.e., no fetal anomalies) in mice.



Unconjugated donidalorsen concentrations in the parental liver of males and females
increased with increasing dose of drug. Unconjugated donidalorsen concentrations in the
fetal liver were below the limit of quantitation in all donidalorsen-treated groups. Notably,
unconjugated donidalorsen concentrations in the placenta (up to 0.31 µg/g) and testes (up to
1.61 µg/g) were much lower than in the liver (i.e., 3 to 43 µg/g for 1 to 10 mg/kg/week
donidalorsen in F0 females on GD 18 and 7 to 47 µg/g for 1 to 10 mg/kg/week for males on
Day 73). It was unclear if donidalorsen or unconjugated donidalorsen crossed the placenta to
reach fetal tissues.



Treatment of F0 male and female mice with mouse surrogate ISIS 722059 at 4 mg/kg/week
statistically decreased liver mRNA expression of KLKB1/PKK by 80% and 75%,
respectively.



The NOAEL for donidalorsen on male and female fertility and mating performance, as well
as developmental toxicity, was the high dose of 10 mg/kg/week.

There were no effects of ISIS 546254 or mouse surrogate ISIS 482584 on estrous cyclicity.

There were no effects of ISIS 546254 or mouse surrogate ISIS 482584 on fertility (mating

At the time of Cesarean section, mean gravid uterus weights were decreased at 10.5, 42, and

13.2.1. Pharmacology
13.2.1.1. Primary Pharmacodynamics
The primary pharmacodynamics of donidalorsen were evaluated in an in vivo primary
pharmacology study in human KLKBl/PKK transgenic mice.
In Vivo Primary Pharmacology Studies
In Vivo Evaluation of ISIS 721744 Activity in Human KLKBl/PKK Transgenic MiceAnalysis of Plasma PKK Protein Levels (ELN 23-100d)
The effects on human PKK plasma protein levels were evaluated following single dose SC
administration of donidalorsen (0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, and 10 mg/kg) to transgenic mice expressing the
human KLKB1/PKK gene. A single dose of donidalorsen reduced plasma PKK protein in human
KLKB1/PKK transgenic mice in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Figure 37). Plasma PKK
protein levels were reduced up to a maximum of about 91% on Day 14 after treatment with
10 mg/kg donidalorsen. After Day 14, plasma PKK protein levels gradually increased to baseline
levels and were restored by Day 42 or Day 56 at 1 mg/kg or 3 mg/kg donidalorsen, respectively.
At Day 56, plasma PKK protein levels at 10 mg/kg were still 20% below baseline levels.
Based on nonlinear curve fit analysis, the median effective dose 50 (ED50) at Days 7 and 14 after
treatment with donidalorsen was 0.67 and 0.75 mg/kg, respectively (Figure 38).

13.2.2. Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism,
Excretion/Pharmacokinetics
The ADME, PK, and TK profiles of donidalorsen were evaluated both in vitro and in vivo (mice
and monkeys).
13.2.2.1. Absorption
The plasma pharmacokinetics of donidalorsen was evaluated in a GLP-compliant single-dose SC
ADME study in rats with radiolabeled [3H]donidalorsen and a GLP-compliant 6-week repeatdose SC study in mice.
ADME of [3H]ISIS 721744 Following a Single Subcutaneous Dose Administration to
Sprague Dawley Rats (Study Nos. IPI/06; 721744-APK02)
Nonpigmented Sprague Dawley rats were treated with single SC doses of [3H]donidalorsen (2 or
10 mg/kg).
Following a single SC dose of [3H]donidalorsen at 2 mg/kg to male nonpigmented Sprague
Dawley rats, Cmax of 0.375 and 0.538 µg equivalent/mL were reached in the blood and plasma,
respectively, at 1 hour for both, after which radioactivity declined in a biphasic manner. The
blood:plasma ratio calculated from AUC0-∞ was 0.76. Cmax (µg equivalent/g) of 24.40 at 24 hours
and 14.89 at 168 hours were reached in the liver and kidney, respectively. Most tissues achieved
concentrations similar to or slightly above the blood radioactivity concentrations. Tissue:blood
ratios at 24 hours were highest in the liver and kidney (1877 and 850, respectively) consistent

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
with uptake of donidalorsen. The thyroid gland, pancreas, large and small intestine, spleen,
lymph node, and bone marrow had tissue:blood ratios between 24.2 to 69.2 at 24 hours.
Following a single SC dose of [3H]donidalorsen at 2 mg/kg to male nonpigmented Sprague
Dawley rats, the mean cumulative recovery (0 to Day 56) of radioactivity in excreta was 76.8%
(17.14% from urine +57.46% from feces +2.16% from cage wash). Residual radioactivity in the
carcass on Day 56 accounted for 5.84% of the administered dose resulting in an overall recovery
of 82.6%.
Following a single SC dose of [3H]donidalorsen at 10 mg/kg to male and female nonpigmented
rats, radioactivity was distributed to tissues by the first sampling time at 2 hours and reached
maximal concentrations within 2 to 48 hours postdose with highest concentrations of
radioactivity in the kidney, liver, intestinal mucosa, salivary gland, bone marrow, lymph nodes,
and splenic red pulp. Concentrations of radioactivity in most organs/tissues decreased by the end
of the sampling period at 336 hours, except for the kidney where radioactivity levels remained at
similar levels throughout the sampling period.
Recovery of radioactivity in urine and feces from nonpigmented rats following a single SC dose
of [3H]donidalorsen at 10 mg/kg was 0.35% and 1.37% of dose, respectively for males and
0.30% and 1.31% of dose, respectively for females.
A 6-Week Subcutaneous Repeat-Dose Pharmacokinetic Study of ISIS 721744 in CD-1 Mice
(Study Nos. G122111; 721744-APK03)
Male ICR mice were treated by SC administration with donidalorsen (10 or 20 mg/kg/week once
weekly) for 6 weeks (Days 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 36, and 43) to determine the PK profile and
distribution of donidalorsen to kidney and liver. As described in the study report, concentrations
of total full-length donidalorsen, including fully conjugated, partially conjugated (minus 1-, 2-,
and 3-GalNAc sugars), and unconjugated donidalorsen (ISIS 780124), were determined in
mouse plasma by a validated hybridization ECL assay, while concentrations of unconjugated
donidalorsen in kidney and liver samples were analyzed by a validated HPLC-MS/MS
bioanalytical method.
Median Tmax was 0.5 hours on Days 1 and 43 at 10 and 20 mg/kg donidalorsen. Mean Cmax and
AUC increased in a slightly greater than dose proportional manner on Days 1 and 43. There was
lack of accumulation after repeat dosing.
Concentrations of unconjugated donidalorsen were higher in the kidney than in the liver.
Concentrations of unconjugated donidalorsen in the liver were similar at 10 and 20 mg/kg/week
possibly due to saturation of tissue uptake at these dose levels.

13.2.2.2. Distribution
The distribution of donidalorsen was evaluated in vitro for the whole blood and plasma

In Vitro Evaluation of Whole Blood and Plasma Concentration Ratio of ISIS 721744

The in vitro mean blood to plasma ratio of donidalorsen (tested neat, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, and

13.2.2.3. Metabolism
The metabolism of donidalorsen was evaluated after single SC administration of
[3H]donidalorsen to rats, as well as from select urine samples from studies in mice, monkeys,
and humans. Further, the metabolism of donidalorsen linker-related metabolites was evaluated in
select plasma, urine, and fecal samples from studies in mice, monkeys, and humans, as well as
from liver and kidney samples from rat.
Metabolite Profiling and Identification Studies Following a Single Subcutaneous Dose
Administration of [3H]ISIS 721744 to Male and Female Rats (Study Nos. IPI/07; 721744APK02)
This study evaluated the metabolic profile of donidalorsen in rat whole blood and plasma, liver
and kidney tissues, and in the excreta (urine and feces) by liquid chromatography mass
spectrometry (LC-MS) after single SC administration of [3H]donidalorsen at 10 mg/kg to male
and female nonpigmented rats.
Donidalorsen was seen in the liver, kidney, plasma, and whole blood. Donidalorsen was the
major component at 2 hours in plasma and blood but was not detected at 24 hours in plasma and
blood. Unconjugated donidalorsen (i.e., ISIS 780124) was the major component in liver (2 and
24 hours) and kidney (24 hours). Two major components were present in the kidney at 2 hours:
unconjugated donidalorsen (i.e., ISIS 780124) and donidalorsen minus 3 GalNAc sugars (i.e.,
ISIS 721744 -3 GalNAc). Two major components were detected in feces samples at 0 to 24
hours: ISIS 780124 3’N-18 and ISIS 780124 3’N-17. Several ISIS 780124 shortmers were
identified as major components in urine at 0 to 24 hours, from ISIS 780124 3’N-10 to ISIS
780124 3’N-14. As described in the study report, all identified metabolites were consistent with
nuclease-mediated metabolism to chain shortened oligonucleotides with full, partial, or without
GalNAc or linker-conjugation.

Metabolic Profiling and Identification of ISIS 721744 Oligonucleotide-Related Metabolites
by HPLC-High-Resolution Mass Spectrometer in Select Urine Samples From Mice,
Monkeys, and Humans (Study Nos. 727-085, 727-081, ISIS 721744-CS1; 721744-IS10)
This study identified donidalorsen oligonucleotide containing metabolites (full-length or chainshortened) from urine samples at steady state from mice, monkeys, and humans treated with
multiple SC doses of donidalorsen (i.e., 10 mg/kg from 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study in
mice [Study No. 721744-AS01]; 30 mg/kg from 39-week repeat-dose toxicity study in monkeys
[Study No. 721744-AS02]; and 80 mg from phase 1 trial in humans with dosing every 4 weeks
for four total doses [Study No. ISIS 721744-CS1]) using liquid chromatography with a tandem
ultraviolet detector and high-resolution mass spectrometer method.
As described in the study report, the oligonucleotide portions of conjugated ASO molecules are
metabolized by hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bonds via endonuclease and/or exonuclease
(either 5' and/or 3') enzymes. Metabolism of the GalNAc-conjugation component of
donidalorsen typically occurs by a sequential loss of the three GalNAc sugar moieties (−1, −2,
and -3 GalNAc), followed by the loss of a portion, or all the remaining THA linker (Shemesh et
al. 2016; Weidolf et al. 2021). Complete loss of the THA linker results in the formation of ISIS
780124, the unconjugated version of donidalorsen. The metabolism of the two portions of
donidalorsen (oligonucleotide and GalNAc) may occur simultaneously resulting in many
potential metabolites with multiple potential metabolic pathways responsible for a single
metabolite compound.

Profiling, Identification, and Quantitation of ISIS 721744 Linker-Related Metabolites by
HPLC-MS/MS in Select Plasma, Urine, and Fecal Samples From Mice, Monkeys, and
Humans (Study No. 721744-IS12)
This study identified linker-only-related metabolites of donidalorsen (no full-length or chainshortened oligonucleotide components) from plasma (monkey and human), urine (mouse,
monkey, and human), and feces (monkey) after SC dosing of donidalorsen (i.e., 2 and/or
10 mg/kg from 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study in mice [Study No. 721744-AS01]; 2 and/or
30 mg/kg from 39-week repeat-dose toxicity study in monkeys [Study No. 721744-AS02]; and
80 mg from phase 1 trial in humans with dosing every 4 weeks for four total doses [Study No.
ISIS 721744-CS1]) by a HPLC-MS/MS method. Eleven total linker metabolites (putative linker
metabolites M4 to M14) were monitored in these studies.
Six linker metabolites were detected in monkey plasma (M5 and M8 to M12) and three linker
metabolites were detected in human plasma (M5, M8, and M12).
Ten linker metabolites (M5 to M14) were similarly detected in mouse, monkey, and human
urine. The linker metabolites with the highest peak area ratios were M8, M5, and M12, which
were consistent across the three species.
Ten linker metabolites (M5 to M14) were detected in monkey feces. The linker metabolites with
the highest peak area ratios were M8, M10, M11, and M5.
As described by the Applicant, the THA-linker-related metabolism is mostly similar across
species with oxidative metabolites being formed and eliminated through urine and bile. The
overall metabolic pathways for the THA-linker-related metabolites of donidalorsen involve
hydrolysis of GalNAc sugars and oligonucleotide moieties to form M4 metabolite, followed by
internal cyclization of M4 to form cyclized linker M5 metabolite which would then undergo
mono- and di-oxidation to form M6 and M7 metabolites. Dephosphorylation of M4 metabolite
resulted in the formation of M8 metabolite followed by sequential oxidation at each branching
arm of M8 metabolite to form mono-, di-, tri-, and tetra-oxidation metabolites (M9 to M12
metabolites). Additional metabolites resulting from dealkylation (M13 metabolite), or
deamination (M14 metabolite) were also detected. The proposed pathway for the metabolism of
linker-related moieties of donidalorsen is shown in Figure 40 (Shemesh et al. 2016).

ongoing. At the time of the pre-NDA meeting, the Division agreed that it would be acceptable to

13.2.3.1. Carcinogenicity
A 6-Month Study of ISIS 721744 by Subcutaneous Bolus Injection in CByB6F1Tg(HRAS)2Jic Hemizygous Transgenic Mouse (Study Nos. 727-140; 721744-AS07)
Key Study Findings


Tg.rasH2 mice (n=25/sex/group) were administered vehicle control (0.9% sodium chloride
for injection), donidalorsen (5, 10, or 20 mg/kg/dose for males and 10, 20, or 60 mg/kg/dose
for females), or mouse surrogate ISIS 722059 (10 mg/kg/dose) Q2W for up to 6 months by
SC injection. A positive control group was included in which Tg.rashH2 mice (10/sex) were
administered urethane (500 mg/kg/dose) via intraperitoneal injection on Days 1, 3, and 5.
The mouse was not a pharmacologically relevant species with donidalorsen, and this study
evaluated off-target effects. The mouse surrogate ISIS 722059 was included to assess
inhibition of PKK and potential on-target effects.



There was no statistically significant increase or decrease in mortality dose response across
the vehicle control and donidalorsen-treated groups, in either male or female mice. The
pairwise comparisons showed a statistically significant decrease in mortality in the male
5 mg/kg/dose group (low dose) compared to the vehicle control group (p=0.0160). The
pairwise comparisons showed no statistically significant increase or decrease in mortality
between the mouse surrogate ISIS 722059 group and the vehicle control group, in either male
or female mice.



There were no donidalorsen-related or mouse surrogate ISIS 722059-related effects on body
weights.



Effects on clinical chemistry included increases in AST, ALT, and glutamate dehydrogenase
in males at 10 and 20 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen and females at 60 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen,
which correlated with histopathology findings in the liver.



A MTD was achieved at the high dose of 20 mg/kg Q2W in males based on histopathology
findings in the liver and elevations of glutamate dehydrogenase. The high dose of 60 mg/kg
Q2W in females did not meet the criteria for an MTD.



Gross pathology findings included liver mass in one male at 5 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen and
one male at 20 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen, which correlated with neoplastic histopathology
findings of hepatocellular adenoma in the liver of both mice.



Neoplastic histopathology findings included hepatocellular adenoma in the liver in 1/25
males at 5 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen, 2/25 males at 20 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen, and 1/25
males at 10 mg/kg/dose ISIS 722059. The hepatocellular adenoma seen in the males at
5 and 20 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen were accompanied by increases in AST and ALT, gross
pathology findings in the liver, and non-neoplastic histopathology findings in the liver of
microvesicular hepatocellular vacuolation, basophilic focus of cellular alteration,
hepatocellular single cell necrosis, and/or basophilic pigmented macrophage. There were no
150

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
correlating gross pathology or non-neoplastic histopathology findings for the male at
10 mg/kg/dose ISIS 722059.


Non-neoplastic histopathology findings were noted in the liver (microvesicular
hepatocellular vacuolation, basophilic pigmented macrophages, hepatocellular single cell
necrosis, karyocytomegaly, and/or basophilic focus of cellular alteration in males at 5, 10,
and/or 20 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen, and/or females at 10, 20, and/or 60 mg/kg/dose
donidalorsen, and/or males and/or females at 10 mg/kg/dose ISIS 722059); kidney (epithelial

vacuolation in females at 60 mg/kg/dose donidalorsen). The histopathology findings were
attributed to or a consequence of oligonucleotide uptake.



The positive control (urethane) group confirmed the carcinogenic responsiveness of the
Tg.rasH2 model. Urethane treatment resulted in a decrease in body weight in both male and
female mice and a statistically significant increase in unscheduled deaths (i.e., decrease in
survival) compared to the vehicle control group in both male and female mice. Neoplastic
findings included hemangiosarcoma (whole body in male and female mice), malignant
lymphoma (hemolymphoreticular tissue in male mice), and bronchioloalveolar adenoma and
carcinoma (lungs in male and female mice). These findings are consistent with known effects
of urethane administration (National Toxicology Program 2021).



Toxicokinetic parameters were not evaluated.



Donidalorsen concentrations in the kidney and liver of males and females were mostly
increased with increasing donidalorsen dose following 6-months of treatment.



Liver PKK mRNA expression was statistically reduced in male and female mice treated with
10 mg/kg/dose ISIS 722059 Q2W for 26 weeks by 94% and 79%, respectively, compared to
controls.



The ECAC concurred with the doses for the study in male mice but could not recommend
doses for female mice. The Applicant did not conduct a new DRF study to identify an
acceptable high dose or seek ECAC concurrence for their final dose selection in female mice.
The ECAC concluded that the carcinogenicity study was adequate for male mice but
inadequate for female mice because a MTD was not achieved and no other valid basis to
support the high dose was discernable.

13.2.3.4. Extractables and Leachables
The donidalorsen drug product is a sterile, single-dose, ready-to-use parenteral solution for SC
administration. The drug product is packaged in a staked needle glass PFS closed with a
(b) (4) rubber plunger stopper. The PFS is assembled into an AI for the final drug
product presentation. The AI delivers a single dose of 80 mg donidalorsen in 0.8 mL
(100 mg/mL). Extractables and leachables studies were conducted to assess the donidalorsen
drug product container closure system, which were evaluated (see Nonclinical Primary Review
dated July 25, 2025). There were no nonclinical safety concerns with the potential leachables
from the primary container closure system of donidalorsen.

14. Clinical Pharmacology
14.1. In Vitro Studies
14.1.1. Metabolism and Excretion of the Antisense
Oligonucleotide Moiety of Donidalorsen (Studies
ISIS 721744-IS10 and ISIS 721744-APK02)
Donidalorsen contains a 2′-O-methoxyethyl (MOE)-modified chimeric gapmer ASO with a
mixed backbone of phosphodiester (PS) and phosphorothioate (PO) internucleotide linkages.
These have been used in previously approved GalNAc-ASO products, such as Eplontersen
(NDA 217388), Nusinersen (NDA 209531), Tegsedi (NDA 211172), and Tofersen (NDA
215887). The ASO moiety of donidalorsen is expected to share the same metabolic pathway as
other approved GalNAc-conjugated ASO moieties with similar modifications in the
oligonucleotide backbone. Therefore, the ASO moiety is majorly metabolized by endo-and
exonucleases in tissues to shortmer oligonucleotide metabolites and minimally modulated by
major cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes (AstraZeneca 2023).
The metabolic profile of ASO related metabolites was evaluated in human plasma and urine
samples collected following four doses of donidalorsen-4 in Trial ISIS721744-CS1 (see
Section 14.2 for more details). Shortmer oligonucleotide metabolites were not detected in plasma
2 hours postdose. Total full length donidalorsen (fully conjugated + partially conjugated +
unconjugated) in urine represents <1% of administered dose collected within 24 hours after the
fourth dose administered every 4 weeks. The metabolic profiling results for human urine showed
that various shortmer metabolites together constitute more than 50% of all drug-related species
detected in urine, while the full-length unconjugated donidalorsen constitutes about 38% of all
drug-related species. Although shortmer metabolites appear to have a slightly higher relative
abundance compared to full length donidalorsen in urine based on the metabolic profiling results,
the percent of the dose excreted as shortmer metabolites in urine is not likely to exceed 30% of
the dose. This is primarily as full-length donidalorsen represented <1% of the dose in human
urine while constituting 38% of all drug-related species detected in urine over 24 hours postdose.
Overall, the fragmented ASO metabolites were slowly formed and were subsequently excreted in
the urine. The renal elimination of ASO and its related metabolites is considered a minor route.

14.1.2. Metabolism and Excretion of Linker and Its
Related Metabolites (Studies ISIS 721744-IS12 and
ISIS 721744-IS16)
The GalNAc moiety is covalently conjugated to the ASO portion of donidalorsen via a THA
linker. The GalNAc conjugate undergoes hydrolysis once distributed to the tissue and is detached
from the parent drug. The GalNAc sugar undergoes endogenous carbohydrate catabolism, while
the THA linker undergoes extensive oxidative metabolism based on a study in animals (monkey

161
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
and rats) (Shemesh et al. 2016). The proposed metabolic pathway for the GalNAc-linker moiety
is shown in Figure 41.
Figure 41. Proposed Metabolic Pathway for Linker Portion of Donidalorsen

Source: Report 721744-IS12

The metabolic profile of the linker portion was assessed in plasma, urine, and feces samples
across species (monkey, mice, and human). In total, 11 GalNAc-linker-related metabolites were
detected from various specimens (i.e., urine, plasma, and feces) across species and the metabolic
profiles were generally consistent across species. Among these metabolites, metabolite M4, the
THA linker, is formed by hydrolysis of the GalNAc sugars and hydrolysis from the ASO moiety.
Metabolite M8 is formed by hydrolysis of the phosphate moiety from the linker M4. M8 can be
further metabolized by oxidation to form other metabolites (M9 to M12).
Of the 11 linker-related metabolites, the 3 metabolites with the highest peak area ratio in human
plasma and urine were M5, M8, and M12. Concentrations of major THA-related metabolites M8
and M12 were quantified in human plasma and urine samples collected following four doses of
donidalorsen-4 from Trial ISIS721744-CS1. The concentrations of THA-related metabolites
were assessed in human plasma at hours 2 and 24, as well as in human urine over 0 to 24 hours.

In human plasma, mean concentrations of M8 and M12 were <2% of those determined for parent
drug. In human urine collected over 24 hours, ≥100-fold higher concentrations of M8 and M12
were observed compared to their plasma concentrations (Table 40). However, the amount of M8
and M12 excreted in the urine over 24 hours only accounted for 6.4% and 2.2% of the total
administered dose, respectively.
In vitro cytochrome P450 phenotyping for linker metabolite M8 was conducted in human liver
microsomes and recombinant CYP enzymes (rCYP1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2D6, 3A4). After
60 minutes incubation with M8 at concentrations of 1µM and 3µM in human liver microsomes,
there was little NADPH-dependent consumption of M8. Following incubation with recombinant
CYP enzymes, M8 remained stable with most recombinant enzymes except rCYP3A4, where an
approximate 30% reduction in M8 was observed after 60 minutes. In a repeat study with
rCYP3A4 using 10µM M8, oxidative metabolites were detected with a low signal to noise ratio.
The study suggests that CYP3A4 may contribute to the metabolism of M8. However, M8 is not
considered a major metabolite as M8 demonstrated a low abundance in human plasma (1.3%
relative to parent drug) and urine (6.4% of administered dose).

14.1.3. Plasma Protein Binding and Distribution
(Studies ISIS 721744-IS03, ISIS 721744-IS05, and
721744-IS11)
The extent of plasma protein binding of donidalorsen was evaluated at three nominal
concentrations of 0.5, 5, and 150 µg/mL in human plasma. The degree of donidalorsen bound to
plasma proteins was similar across all concentrations and was ≥98%.
The potential interaction of donidalorsen with warfarin and ibuprofen due to plasma protein
binding was assessed in vitro using an ultrafiltration method. The plasma protein binding of
donidalorsen at 1 µg/mL was similar irrespective of the presence of warfarin (30 µg/mL) and
ibuprofen (300 µg/mL), while the plasma protein binding of warfarin at 3 µg/mL or ibuprofen at
30 µg/mL was also similar irrespective of the presence of donidalorsen (10 µg/mL).
The blood-to-plasma ratio was assessed at six concentrations (0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, and
2 µg/mL) in human whole blood incubated over approximately 1 hour. At all evaluated
concentrations, the blood-to-plasma distribution ratio of donidalorsen was between 0.63 to 0.82,
suggesting that donidalorsen mostly distributes in the plasma compartment.

14.1.4. Drug-Drug Interaction Potential for
Donidalorsen (Studies ISIS 721744-IS06, ISIS
721744-IS07, and ISIS 721744-IS09)
An in vitro study was conducted with cryopreserved human primary hepatocytes to assess the
potential of donidalorsen to induce CYP1A2, CYP2B6, and CYP3A4. The study demonstrated
that donidalorsen did not cause induction of mRNA of these CYP enzymes in all three donors up
to 30µM after 48 hours of incubation. The concentration of 30µM is around 43-fold higher than

peak donidalorsen plasma concentration (around 0.7µM) and is also higher than the Applicant’s
estimated liver concentration of donidalorsen (<10µM) following administration of 80 mg Q4W.
An in vitro study was conducted with cryopreserved human primary hepatocytes to evaluate
cellular uptake of donidalorsen and the inhibition potential of donidalorsen on CYP1A2,
CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, and CYP3A4. The uptake of
donidalorsen into hepatocytes at 1, 10, and 50µM were up to 4.73µM, 12.3µM, and 43.3µM at
120 minutes, suggesting high cellular uptake during the 120-minute incubation period. The
inhibition study results indicated that donidalorsen did not inhibit these CYP enzymes in human
hepatocytes at concentrations up to 50µM.
An in vitro study was conducted with transporter-transfected cells (Madin-Darby Canine Kidney
[MDCK-II]) compared to control cells for solute carrier family and adenosine triphosphate
binding cassette transporters or BSEP vesicles made from Spodoptera frugiperda 9 membrane, to
assess the potential of donidalorsen as an inhibitor or a substrate of major transporters. At a
concentration of 100µM, donidalorsen is not considered as an inhibitor of human organic anion
transporter (OAT) 1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 1, OCT2, organic anion
transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, OATP1B3, MATE1, MATE2-K, Breast Cancer
Resistance Protein (BCRP), P-glycoprotein (P-gp), and BSEP transporters. Donidalorsen is also
not a substrate for OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MATE1, MATE2-K,
and BSEP under the study conditions.
When assessing donidalorsen (10µM) as a substrate of P-gp and BCRP, the concentration of
donidalorsen in all the receiver wells for apical to basolateral flux (absorption) were below lower
limit of quantification (LLOQ =1nM). Some of the receiver wells for basolateral to apical flux
(efflux) were below LLOQ, while some had concentrations slightly above the LLOQ ranging
from 1.1 to 2.7nM. The efflux ratio in BCRP or P-gp transfected MDCK-II cells cannot be
determined. The results in control cells (without BCRP or P-gp) were also similar. The potential
of donidalorsen as a substrate of BCRP and P-gp is low.

14.1.5. Drug-Drug Interaction Potential for Linker
Related Metabolite M8 (Studies ISIS 721744-IS13,
ISIS 721744-IS14, and ISIS 721744-IS15)
An in vitro study was conducted with human hepatic microsomal CYP enzymes (CYP1A2, 2B6,
2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, and CYP3A4/5) to assess the potential of major linker-related inactive
metabolite M8 to act as an inhibitor of human CYP enzymes. Detectable inhibition was only
observed for CYP2B6, 2C9, 2C19, and CYP3A4 (with midazolam or testosterone as probe
substrates) at concentrations up to 100µM. In all cases, IC50 values were >100µM. No shift in
IC50 was noted when enzymes were pre-incubated with M8 in the absence or presence of
NADPH.
An in vitro study was conducted in cryopreserved human hepatocytes to assess the induction
potential of M8 on CYP1A2, CYP2B6, and CYP3A4 following 48 hours incubation. M8 did not
induce CYP1A2, CYP2B6, or CYP3A4 mRNA at concentrations up to 100μM across three
donors.
164
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
An in vitro study was conducted to assess M8 as an inhibitor or a substrate of human OAT1,
OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MATE1, MATE2-K, BCRP, P-gp, and BSEP. The
assay used MDCK-II cells expressing the transporter of interest or a control vector, except for
the BSEP assay, which used Spodoptera frugiperda 9 membrane vesicles expressing human
BSEP.
M8 was not found to be a substrate for OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, OATP1B1, MATE1,
MATE2-K, BCRP, and P-gp under the study conditions. However, M8 is a substrate for
OATP1B3 and BSEP with >2-fold of uptake of M8 observed. As M8 is low in abundance in
systemic circulation (1.3% relative to parent drug), the inhibition of BSEP or OATP1B3 is not
likely to result in clinically meaningful changes in M8 systemic concentrations. However, the
impact on M8 concentrations in the liver is unclear.
At an M8 concentration of 100μM (about 300-fold higher than concentrations observed in human
urine collected over 24 hours post dose [mean concentration 299nM]), 62.9% inhibition was
observed for MATE1 (IC50 of 62.7μM). For the remaining transporters evaluated, the mean
percent inhibition ranged from 6.30% (OAT3) to 46.1% (BSEP). Therefore, M8 is not
considered as an inhibitor of OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MATE2-K,
BCRP, P-gp, and BSEP at 100μM. As M8 demonstrates a low abundance in human plasma and
is minorly excreted in urine (6.4% of total dose over 24 hours), the potential of M8 to inhibit
MATE1 in vivo is low.

14.2.1. Trial CS1
Trial Design
CS1 was a phase 1, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation trial
conducted in healthy adult subjects. The objective of the trial was to evaluate the safety,
tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of donidalorsen following multiple doses
of donidalorsen administered subcutaneously. Eight subjects (six active and two placebo) each
were randomized to the following four cohorts:


Cohort A: 20 mg SC every 4 weeks for 12 weeks (total: 4 doses)



Cohort B: 40 mg SC every 4 weeks for 12 weeks (total: 4 doses)



Cohort C: 60 mg SC every 4 weeks for 12 weeks (total: 4 doses)



Cohort D: 80 mg SC every 4 weeks for 12 weeks (total: 4 doses)

SC doses were administered using a 100 mg/mL solution in a single use vial. Doses were
administered on alternating sites (arm for first and third dose, and abdomen for second and fourth
(b) (6) ) received the second dose in abdomen and third dose in thigh.
dose). One subject (
PK, PD, and ADA Sampling Time
Blood samples for assessing plasma donidalorsen concentration was collected at Day 1 (pre-first
dose and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 12-hour postdose), Day 2 (24-hour post-first dose), Day 3
(48-hour postdose), Day 8 (anytime), and Day 15 (anytime) as well as at Day 85 (pre-fourth dose
and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 12-hour postdose), and Day 86 (24-hour post-fourth dose).
Urine samples for assessing donidalorsen concentrations were collected over 24 hours after the
first (Day 1) and fourth dose (Day 85).
Blood samples for assessing plasma PKK samples were collected at Screening, Day 1 (predose),
Day 15, Day 29 (predose), Day 43, Day 57 (predose), Day 71, Day 85 (predose), Day 92, Day
99, Day 141, and Day 176.
Blood samples for assessing ADAs were collected at Day 1 (predose), Day 15, Day 29 (predose),
Day 92, and Day 176.
PK Results
A total of 32 subjects were randomized and completed the trial. The mean (SD) age was
56 (9) years. The mean (SD) body weight was 80.6 (12.8) kg. The mean body weight is
consistent across treatment groups.
The plasma donidalorsen concentrations were analyzed based on full-length ASO concentration,
which included fully conjugated, partially conjugated (i.e., donidalorsen with 1, 2, or 3 GalNAc
sugar deletions), and unconjugated donidalorsen. See Section 14.3 for details about the
bioanalytical assay.

Immunogenicity Results
In total, 4 out of 26 subjects (16.7%) who received donidalorsen tested positive for ADA. Of
these four subjects, two received 40 mg donidalorsen, and two received 60 mg donidalorsen.
Given the small sample size, the impact of immunogenicity on pharmacokinetics and
pharmacodynamics was inconclusive.

14.2.2. Trial CS9
Trial Design
Trial CS9 was a phase 1, single dose, single site, randomized, open-label, 2-period, 2-sequence,
2-treatment, crossover, bioequivalence trial evaluated at one dose level (donidalorsen 80 mg) in
adult healthy subjects. Participants entered an up to 28-day Screening Period. Following
Screening, 78 eligible participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to one of two treatment
sequences. Subjects received donidalorsen 80 mg administered via subcutaneous injection
(abdomen only) using either an AI or a single-use vial (syringe with manual injection): Sequence
1 (Treatment Period 1: AI and Treatment Period 2: vial) or Sequence 2 (Treatment Period 1: vial
and Treatment Period 2: AI). Participants were administered donidalorsen 80 mg once at the
beginning of each Treatment Period. Treatment Period 2 dosing began at least 28 days but no
more than 42 days after Treatment Period 1 dosing.
The drug products used in this trial included a vialed product that contained 100 mg/mL
donidalorsen (0.8 mL per vial) and an AI that contained 100 mg/mL with a deliverable volume
of 0.8 mL. The AI is the proposed to-be-marketed (TBM) product.

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
PK, PD, and ADA Sampling Time
PK blood samples were collected on Day 1 of each Treatment Period at predose (0 hour) and
0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48, 72, 96, 168, and 336 hour postdose. Samples
were also collected in the Post-Treatment Follow-Up Period at Day 28, 56, and 91/early
termination following last dose of trial drug administration (Treatment Period 2).
PD blood samples were collected within 1 hour prior to dosing on Day 1 during both Treatment
Period 1 and 2. In addition, blood samples were collected on Day 4, Day 8, and Day 15 for
Treatment Period 1.
ADA samples were not collected.
PK Results
A total of 78 subjects were randomized and dosed in the trial. Among them, 76 subjects
completed the trial and two subjects (ID: (b) (6) and (b) (6) ) discontinued the treatment early due to
ineligibility. The mean (SD) baseline body weight for randomized subjects was 77.6 (12.9) kg
and mean (SD) age was 43.1 (12.6) years. The mean body weight is consistent across treatment
groups. The mean plasma concentration time profile by formulation and bioequivalence analysis
are shown Figure 47 and Table 46, respectively. Administration of donidalorsen via AI yielded
comparable Cmax and AUC0-336h as compared with the vialed product. For both parameters, the
geometric mean ratio point estimates and 90% confidence intervals were contained within the
80% to 125% range.

14.2.3. Trial CS2
Trial Design
Trial CS2 was conducted in two parts concurrently with different designs. Part A was
randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled while Part B was open-label. Subjects were
allocated into Part A and B according to type of HAE (HAE Type I or II in Part A and HAE
Type III in Part B). In Part A, 20 subjects were randomized 2:1 to receive SC injection of
donidalorsen 80 mg or placebo every 4 weeks (weeks 1, 5, 9, and 13). In Part B, three subjects
were administered open-label SC injections of donidalorsen-4 and completed the trial. The
treatment duration was 12 weeks. After completing the Treatment Period, subjects had the option
of enrolling in open-label extension Trial CS3 (refer to Section 14.2.5).
PK, PD, and ADA Sampling Time
PK samples were collected at predose, and 1, 2, 4, and 6 hours postdose on Day 1 and Day 85 in
the PK subgroup. For all subjects, predose samples were collected on Day 29, 57, and anytime
on Day 15, and during the Post-Treatment Period (Days 113, 141, and 176).
PD samples were collected at predose on Days 1, 29, 57, 85, and anytime on Day 15 and during
the Post-Treatment Period (Days 113, 141, and 176).
Immunogenicity samples were collected at predose on Days 1, 29, and 57 and anytime on Day
15 and during the Post-Treatment Period (Day 113 and Day 176).

PK Results
A total of 20 subjects with HAE Type I or II (6 in placebo and 14 in donidalorsen) were
randomized in Part A, while 3 subjects with HAE Type III received donidalorsen in Part B. The
mean age was and 38.5 (13.9) and 34 (7.9) years for Parts A and B, respectively. The mean (SD)
body weight was 83.4 (18.4) and 95.7 (8.2) kg for Parts A and B, respectively.
In a small PK subgroup from Part A (N=4) who had more intensive samples collected postdose
on Day 1 and Day 85, the PK parameters are summarized in Table 50.

Similar to results observed in CS1, there was no accumulation following administration of
multiple doses and the median Tmax was observed at around 1 hour postdose. However, the Cmax
in Trial CS2 on Days 1 and 85 was 2- to 3-fold lower compared to that in Trial CS1 following
administration of the same dosing regimen (i.e., donidalorsen-4; Cmax values of 0.592 µg/mL and
0.718 µg/mL on Days 1 and 85, respectively). The Applicant attributed the cross-trial difference
in part to different median body weights across the two trials (91 kg for PK subgroup in Trial
CS2 versus 75 kg in Trial CS1). However, a definitive conclusion cannot be drawn due to small
sample size (N=4) and less intensive postdose sampling in Trial CS2.
No subjects from Part B had intensive PK samples collected. The range of trough concentrations
between Part A and Part B was similar during the Treatment Period, as shown in Figure 51.
However, the limited sample size from Part B limits interpretation of the data.

subjects (N=2) in Part B with PD data limits the interpretation of the data.

Immunogenicity Results
In subjects treated with donidalorsen (Part A and B), the proportion of the ADA-positive patient
rate was 52.9% (9 out of 17 subjects). This included three subjects (17.6%) with pre-existing
antibodies (ADA titers for these subjects did not increase more than 4-fold from baseline after
treatment) and six subjects (35.3%, including two subjects with HAE Type III) with treatmentemergent ADA. The overall median onset of the ADA response in subjects who tested positive
for ADA was Day 15 with a range of 1 to 118 days.
The plasma PKK trough concentrations over time by overall immunogenicity irrespective of
baseline ADA titers is shown in Table 52. At Week 17, subjects with positive ADA had lower
percent reduction from baseline.

Both subjects with HAE Type I or II (Part A, N=14) and subjects with HAE Type III (Part B,

donidalorsen (Run-In Period: 2.82 and Week-1-to-Week-17 period: 0.23). Thus, the assessment
of ADA impact on efficacy may be confounded by different responses to donidalorsen treatment
among patients with different types of HAE.

14.2.4. Trial CS5
Trial Design
For full details on the design of Trial CS5, refer to Section 6.
A vialed presentation (100 mg/mL of donidalorsen, 0.8 mL per vial) was used for administration
of donidalorsen in Trial CS5. Alternate injection administration sites (arm, abdomen, and thigh)
were used for some subjects during the Treatment Period.
PK, PD, and ADA Sampling Time
Samples for assessing plasma donidalorsen concentrations were collected at predose and 2 hours
postdose on Day 1 (Week 1) and Day 141 (Week 21) for the donidalorsen-4 group or Day 113
(Week 17) for the donidalorsen-8 group. Additional samples were collected at predose on Days
29, 57, 85, and 113 (i.e., Week 5, 9, 13, 17) as well as up to 13 weeks post-last dose.
Samples for assessing plasma PKK samples were collected predose at Days 1, 29, 57, 85, 113,
141, and 169 (i.e., Week 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, and 25) as well as up to 13 weeks post-last dose.
ADA samples were collected at Days 1, 29, 85, 141, and 169 (i.e., Week 1, 5, 13, 21, and 25) as
well as 4 and 13 weeks post last dose.
PK Results
The 2-hour postdose donidalorsen concentrations were similar between donidalorsen-4 and
donidalorsen-8 groups on both Day 1 (Week 1) and Day 141 (Week 21) or Day 113 (Week 17),
as reported in Table 54. The geometric mean trough concentrations on Day 113 (Week 17) were
around 2-fold higher in the donidalorsen-4 group than in the donidalorsen-8 group, although high
PK variability was noted.

attributable to the overall lower reduction in PKK concentrations in the donidalorsen-8 group.

Immunogenicity Results
In the donidalorsen-4 group, 12 (26.7%) subjects were positive for ADA, 4 of whom were
positive at baseline. In the donidalorsen-8 group, seven (30.4%) subjects were positive for ADA,
two of whom (8.7%) were positive at baseline. In total, nine (20%) and five (21.7%) subjects had
treatment-emergent ADAs in the donidalorsen-4 and donidalorsen-8 groups, respectively. Of
note, subjects with treatment-emergent ADAs included subjects who were ADA-negative at
baseline and developed ADAs during the Treatment Period as well as subjects who were ADApositive at baseline and ADA titers increased during the Treatment Period.

Treatment-Emergent ADA: Includes both Treatment-Induced and Treatment-Boosted ADA-positive subjects.
Treatment-Induced ADA: ADA developed de novo (seroconversion) following trial drug administration (i.e., formation of ADA any
time after the initial drug administration in a subject without pre-existing ADA, i.e., baseline negative ADA).
Treatment-Boosted ADA: Pre-existing ADA that were boosted to a higher level following trial drug administration (i.e., any time after
the initial drug administration the ADA titer is greater than the baseline titer by a factor of 8-fold or more).
Treatment-Unaffected ADA: Pre-existing ADA that were not affected (boosted) following trial drug administration (i.e., any time after
the initial drug administration the ADA titer is less than 8-fold).
Negative ADA: All evaluated immunogenicity sample results during the Treatment and Post-Treatment Periods were negative and
subjects were to have at least one evaluable immunogenicity result collected after the first dose of trial drug. If a subject had only a
positive sample at Baseline (Day 1 predose) and was negative at all other time points, the subject had a negative immunogenicity
status.

14.2.5. Trial CS3
Trial Design
Trial CS3 is an ongoing OLE trial of phase 2 double-blind Trial CS2 (referred to as the Index
Trial) to evaluate the long-term safety, efficacy, and alternative dosing of donidalorsen. Subjects
from Trial CS2 were enrolled into Trial CS3 if they successfully completed qualification
procedures and in the opinion of the investigator, the subject would benefit from continued
treatment.
The trial consisted of four periods including the Qualification Period, a Treatment Period, an
Extended Treatment Period, and a Post-Treatment Period. The Treatment Period was composed
of a Fixed Dosing Period and a Flexible Dosing Period during which the donidalorsen dosage for
each subject could be changed.
All eligible subjects were to receive donidalorsen-4 from Week 1 to Week 13 (Fixed Dosing
Period). Following completion of the first 12-week period, subjects (based on the Investigator
and Sponsor Medical Monitor recommendation) had three different dosing options starting at
Week 17 (Flexible Dosing Period):


Subjects could continue receiving donidalorsen-4.



For subjects who were attack free for ≥12 weeks after entering this OLE Trial (the Fixed
Dosing Period), the investigator could initiate a dose at a reduced frequency of donidalorsen8. The reduced frequency dosing could begin at any trial visit starting at or after Week 17. If
a subject’s disease was not adequately controlled on donidalorsen-8, then dosing could return
to donidalorsen-4.



For subjects who were not attack free for ≥12 weeks after entering this OLE Trial (the Fixed
Dosing Period), the investigator could initiate a higher dose of donidalorsen at 100 mg every
4 weeks. The higher dose could begin at any trial visit starting at or after Week 17. If subjects
developed any tolerability or safety issue during treatment, the dose could be reduced back to
donidalorsen-4.

At the end of the 52-week Treatment Period (Fixed Dosing + Flexible Dosing), subjects had the
option of receiving donidalorsen in an Extended Treatment Period (during which flexible dosing
was maintained) for up to an additional 156 weeks (approximately 3 years) for a Total Treatment
Period (Treatment + Extended Treatment) of up to approximately 209 weeks (approximately 4
years), or enter the 12-week Post-Treatment Period.

PK, PD, and ADA Sampling Time
PK, PD, and ADA blood samples were collected at predose at Weeks 1, 5, 9, and 13 in the Fixed
Dosing Period, and at predose at Weeks 21, 29, 37, 45, and 53 in the Flexible Dosing Period, and
anytime in the Post-Treatment Period (Week 65).
In the Extended Treatment Period Year 2, PK, PD, and ADA blood samples were collected at
predose at Weeks 65, 77, 89, 105, and anytime in the Post-Treatment Period (Week 113).
In the Extended Treatment Period Year 3, PK, PD, and ADA blood samples were collected at
predose at Weeks 117, 129, 141, 157, and anytime in the Post-Treatment Period (at Week 169).
PK Results
In this OLE trial, 20 subjects were enrolled from Index Trial CS2 and received the trial drug,
including 17 subjects with HAE Type I/II (12 from Index Q4W and 5 from Index placebo) and 3
subjects with HAE Type III. This interim CSR describes data collected as of the data cutoff date
of February 26, 2024. At the time of data cutoff, 15 subjects completed ≥2 years of trial drug,
and 14 subjects completed ≥3 years of trial drug. During the Flexible Dosing Period, eight
subjects with HAE Type I or II changed dosing frequency from donidalorsen-4 during the Fixed
(b) (6)
Dosing Period to donidalorsen-8. However, three subjects (
) returned to a donidalorsen-4 dosing frequency due to experiencing an HAE attack. The
remaining five subjects remained on a donidalorsen-8 dosing frequency.
The mean plasma trough concentration over time during the Fixed Dosing Period (Week 1 to
Week 13 of Trial CS3) is shown in Figure 59. In the Index Placebo group (i.e., did not receive
donidalorsen until Trial CS3), the trough concentrations reached steady state by Day 57 (Week
9) following administration of donidalorsen-4. In the Index Q4W group (for both HAE Type I/II
and Type III), trough concentrations were relatively stable from the beginning of the Fixed
Dosing Period, indicating no significant accumulation of donidalorsen in plasma over time.

During the Fixed Dosing Period in which all subjects received donidalorsen-4 dosing, the HAE

Immunogenicity Results
The ADA incidence rate was 70.6% (12 out of 17 subjects) in the overall HAE Type I/II group
(4 from Index Placebo and 8 from Index Q4W), out of which 11 subjects (64.7%) had treatmentemergent ADAs, and 1 subject (5.9%) had treatment-unaffected ADAs (pre-existing ADAs that
were not boosted following drug administration). Among subjects with HAE Type III, the
incidence rate of treatment-emergent ADAs was 100% (three out of three subjects). ADApositive subjects who rolled over from Trial CS2 remained ADA-positive in Trial CS3.

14.2.6. Trial CS7
Trial Design
Trial CS7 is an ongoing open-label trial to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of
donidalorsen in subjects with Type I and II HAE. Two treatment arms were evaluated:


OLE subjects who rolled over from Trial CS5 (referred to as the Index Trial).



Donidalorsen-naïve subjects who were previously maintained on other HAE prophylactic
therapies (i.e., lanadelumab, berotralstat, or a C1-esterase inhibitor).

The trial consists of four periods, including a Qualification Period for OLE subjects (Week −4 to
−1) or a Screening Period for new subjects who switched from other HAE prophylactic therapies
(Week −10 to −1), a Treatment Period (Week 1 to 53), an Extended Treatment Period (Week 54
to 157), and a Post-Treatment Period (end of treatment +13 weeks).
For OLE subjects who rolled over from Index Trial CS5 (OLE subjects), subjects who were
previously treated with donidalorsen-4 or placebo Q4W in Trial CS5 received donidalorsen-4
beginning 28±3 days after the last dose received in Trial CS5. Subjects who were previously
treated with donidalorsen-8 in Trial CS5 received donidalorsen-8 in Trial CS7 beginning 56±3
days after last dose in Trial CS5, unless they were not attack free for ≥8 weeks (Week 17 to 25 of
Trial CS5), in which case they received donidalorsen-4. If subjects participated in the Extended
Treatment Period (Week 54 to Week 157), they could change dosing frequency (from
donidalorsen-8 to donidalorsen-4 or from donidalorsen-4 to donidalorsen-8), as determined by
clinical symptoms (per investigator).
For donidalorsen-naive subjects who switched from other HAE prophylactic treatments (Switch
Subjects), subjects were treated with donidalorsen-4 during the Treatment Period and had the
option to change dose frequency based on clinical symptoms (per investigator). Switch Subjects
had to be on a stable dose of prophylaxis treatment with lanadelumab, berotralstat, or a C1esterase inhibitor for at least 12 weeks prior to the Screening Period and were to continue taking
their HAE prophylactic treatment during the Screening Period. The schedule to switch from
other prophylactic treatments to donidalorsen is as follows:


Lanadelumab: Subject was to take last dose of lanadelumab 14 days ±3 days prior to Day 1.



Berotralstat: Subject was to continue taking a stable dose of berotralstat for 14 days ±3 days
after Day 1.



C1-esterase inhibitor: Subject was to continue taking a stable dose of C1-esterase inhibitor
for 14 days ±3 days after Day 1.

PK, PD, ADA Sampling Time

Plasma samples for assessing pharmacokinetics (donidalorsen plasma concentrations),
pharmacodynamics (plasma PKK concentrations) and ADA were collected at predose on

The cross-reactivity of the assay was assessed with three putative metabolites ISIS 834440, ISIS
834441, and ISIS 834443, which are 19-mer, 10-mer, and 5-mer metabolites of unconjugated
donidalorsen. There was a 105% cross-reactivity with ISIS 834440 (19-mer metabolite of
unconjugated donidalorsen), while there was only <0.267% cross-relativity with both ISIS
834441 (10-mer metabolite) and ISIS 834443 (5-mer metabolite). The cross-reactivity potential
with 19-mer metabolites may affect the assessment of systemic exposure of full length
donidalorsen. However,19-mer metabolite was not present either in the plasma collected at
2 hours postdose based on Trial CS01-BA04 or in pooled human urine collected over 24 hours
after fourth monthly dose of donidalorsen based on Trial 721744-IS10. Although cross-reactivity
with other chain-shortened metabolites from 18-mer to 11-mer were not assessed, 11-mer to 18mer metabolites were not found in the plasma collected at 2 hours postdose based on Trial CS01BA04. The data suggest that interference due to the presence of these chain shortened
metabolites is not likely.

values. The correction factor was used to justify the difference in antibody concentrations among
different commercial kit lots. The difference among different commercial lots was first
discovered during the analysis of samples from Trial CS5, when endogenous quality control
concentrations obtained from new kit lots demonstrated consistently lower PKK concentrations
compared to historical data. A correction factor was therefore used to correct the new sample
concentrations using the new kits lot and resulted in consistent values within ±20% of reference
results obtained using the qualified kit lots, as shown in Figure 64.

14.4. Immunogenicity Assessment—Impact of
PK/PD, Efficacy, and Safety
Immunogenicity of donidalorsen was evaluated in a phase 1 trial (CS1) in healthy subjects as
well as in four trials in subjects with HAE (CS2, CS3, CS5, and CS7). Refer to the
immunogenicity assay review by the Office of Pharmaceutical Quality Research for details
regarding the immunogenicity assay validation (DARRTS reference ID: 5643653). The ADA
assay is generally acceptable, and data is interpretable.

210
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
Treatment-emergent ADAs were assessed. The definition of treatment-emergent ADAs included
both treatment-induced ADAs, defined as ADAs developed de novo following drug
administration in a subject without pre-existing ADAs; and treatment-boosted ADAs, defined as
pre-existing ADAs that were boosted to a higher-level following drug administration (i.e., any
time after the initial drug administration the ADA titer is greater than baseline titer by a factor of
8-fold or more).
The incidence rate of treatment-emergent ADAs was 16.7% following administration of
donidalorsen 20 to 80 mg once every 4 weeks for 12 weeks in healthy participants (Trial CS1,
dose-dependence not observed), 35.3% following donidalorsen 80 mg once every 4 weeks for 12
weeks in subjects with HAE (Trial CS2), and 20% to 22% following donidalorsen 80 mg once
every 4 weeks or every 8 weeks for 24 weeks in subjects with HAE (Trial CS5), respectively.
The incidence rate of treatment-emergent ADAs was generally consistent across populations and
similar between the donidalorsen-4 and donidalorsen-8 regimens. Treatment-emergent ADAs
were characterized with a median onset ranging from 15 days to 175 days postdose and median
peak titer ranged from 25 to 800. A summary of immunogenicity incidence rates and peak titers
across trials is shown in Table 70.

Impact of Immunogenicity on Pharmacokinetics
Based on results from Trial CS5 and Trial CS7, an increase in Ctrough was observed in some
ADA-positive subjects who also had high ADA titers. The increase in Ctrough was noted in some
Rollover subjects from Trial CS5 who continued receiving the same dosing regimen of
donidalorsen-4 in Trial CS7. These subjects also experienced an increase in ADA titers during
Trial CS7. There is likely an association between presence of ADA and increased Ctrough,ss,
possibly due to the binding of ADAs to donidalorsen which extended its plasma half-life. See
Section 14.2.6 for more details.

Impact of Immunogenicity on Efficacy
There was no apparent effect of ADAs on efficacy based on the HAE attack rate observed in
Trial CS5 and Trial CS7. However, the small sample size of ADA-positive subjects precludes
making a definitive conclusion. See Sections 14.2.4 and 14.2.6 for more details.
Impact of Immunogenicity on Safety
In Trial CS5, a higher proportion of ADA-positive subjects who received donidalorsen-4
reported injection site reactions, while no ADA-positive subjects from the donidalorsen-8 group
reported injection site reactions. Although a higher peak ADA titer was observed among subjects
in the donidalorsen-4 group compared to that in the donidalorsen-8 group, the peak titer was
reported by Week 13 to Week 21, which was later than the time of the first injection site reaction
reported in most subjects. There is thus no clear temporal association between high ADA titers
and the onset of injection site reactions. Given the small sample size, a definitive conclusion on
the impact of ADAs on safety cannot be drawn. See Section 14.2.4 for more details.
In Trial CS7, a trend of increase in Ctrough was observed in subjects with high ADA titers
(b) (6) ) who had very high ADA titers (102400) during Trial CS7
(>1000). One subject (
reported an anaphylaxis reaction after the date of NDA data cutoff. The association between high

14.5.1.2. Introduction
The primary objectives of Applicant’s analysis were to:


Develop a population PK model of donidalorsen using data from healthy volunteers and
patients with HAE.



Develop a population PK/PD model using data from healthy volunteers and patients with
HAE.



Perform simulations using the final models to support dose selection.
14.5.1.3. Model Development
14.5.1.3.1. Data

PK Data
The PK analyses for donidalorsen were based on PK data from one phase 1 trial in healthy
subjects, one bioequivalence trial, one phase 2 trial, and one phase 3 trial in patients with HAE.
Brief descriptions of the trials included are presented in Table 72.
The below limit of quantification (BLQ) samples were excluded from the population PK
modeling. It seems to be reasonable to exclude BLQ samples due to the low percent of BLQ
samples (<5%). The final NONMEM data file for donidalorsen PK model development
contained 4242 donidalorsen observations from 177 subjects, including 101 healthy volunteers
and 76 HAE patients.
Table 73 provides summary statistics of the baseline demographic covariates in the PK analysis
dataset.
PD Data
The PK/PD analyses for donidalorsen were based on PK/PD data from one phase 1 trial in
healthy subjects, one bioequivalence trial, one phase 2 trial, and one phase 3 trial in patients with
HAE. Brief descriptions of the trials included are presented in Table 72.
The BLQ samples were excluded from the population PK/PD modeling. It seems to be
reasonable to exclude BLQ samples due to the low percent of BLQ samples (<5%). The final
NONMEM data file for donidalorsen PK/PD model development contained 1159 donidalorsen
observations from 177 subjects, including 101 healthy volunteers and 76 HAE patients.

14.5.1.3.2. Base Model
PK Base Model
The population PK model was developed using a nonlinear mixed-effects modeling approach in
Phoenix NLME (Version 8.4). The structural base model was initially developed using data from
Trials ISIS 721744-CS1, ISIS 721744-CS2, and ISIS 721744-CS9 followed by a graphical
assessment of covariates including weight, disease status, site of administration, and drug
presentation on relevant PK parameters. The PK data from subjects in Trial ISIS 721744-CS5
was then included in the base model development.
Interindividual variability was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for individual level
random effects. Residual variability was described using additive error model on log-transformed
data. The quality of the model fit was assessed by diagnostic plots.
PK/PD Base Model
Considering the mechanism of action, an indirect response model was fitted initially to describe
the relationship between donidalorsen concentrations and PKK. The population PK/PD model
was developed in a similar manner to the population PK model (i.e., sequentially based on
available data) and covariates were considered for inclusion into the base model before including
data from Trial ISIS 721744-CS5. The PD parameters were estimated using the sequential model
building method.
14.5.1.3.3. Covariate Analysis
For both PK and PK/PD models, covariate analysis was performed before and after including
data from Trial ISIS 721744-CS5 as described under base model development. Covariates of
interest were tested using a forward addition process followed by backward elimination. For
forward addition and backward elimination, significance levels of 0.01 and 0.001 were utilized,
respectively.
Continuous covariates were evaluated using a power function with the parameter of interest
centered at the median value of the covariate in the population. Categorical covariates were
parameterized using a proportional structure with the most common level of the covariate being
the reference. In addition to covariates in Table 73, covariates evaluated in the development of
the PK model included drug presentation and site of administration. The impact of ADA on
donidalorsen pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics was explored graphically. No apparent
impact of ADA on Cmax was observed, though increased Ctrough was observed in some ADApositive subjects. No apparent impact of ADA on PKK concentrations was observed. PK
samples at and beyond the onset of ADA were excluded from the population PK analysis dataset
due to lack of correlation between antisense oligonucleotide exposure in liver and plasma.

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)

Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
14.5.1.4. Final Model
14.5.1.4.1. PK Final Model
A 2-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination adequately described the PK
data of donidalorsen (Figure 66 and Figure 67). Statistically significant covariate effects on PK
model parameters were the following: body weight on CL/F, Vc/F, Q/F, and Vp/F; site of
administration and drug presentation on ka; and disease status on Vc/F and Q/F. Age, sex, race,
ethnicity, geographical region, mild hepatic impairment, and mild renal impairment are not
significant covariates. The parameter estimates for the final PK model are listed in Table 74. The
RSE for all parameters except covariate of site of administration on ka, covariate of drug
presentation on ka, correlation between CL/F and ka, correlation between Q/F and ka, and
correlation between Vp/F and ka was <30%. All parameters had RSE <41%. Moderate etashrinkage (<25%) was observed for all parameters.
The effects of body weight, disease status, drug presentation, and site of administration on the
AUCτ,ss, Cmax,ss, and Ctrough,ss of donidalorsen are explored in Figure 68. Body weight was the
most influential covariate on PK exposure. The effect of body weight on donidalorsen
pharmacokinetics is unlikely to be clinically meaningful due to lack of exposure-response
relationship for efficacy and safety. The effects of other covariates are generally small, and
unlikely to be clinically meaningful.

14.5.1.4.2. PK/PD Final Model
The final PK/PD model was an indirect effect Emax model with inhibition on the rate of PKK
production by donidalorsen. Statistically significant covariate effects on PD model parameters
were disease status on baseline PKK and IC50. The pooled PD data were adequately described by
the final model (Figure 69 and Figure 70). The parameter estimates for the final model are listed
in Table 75. The RSE for all parameters were <30%. The precision of parameter estimates is
reasonable. Eta-shrinkage was low to moderate for baseline (10.0%), IC50 (11.7%), and kout
(28.6%). The covariate effect of disease status on the maximum PKK percent change from
baseline (nadir) over the steady-state dosing interval and PKK percent change from baseline at
the PK Ctrough,ss were within the 80% to 125% range (Figure 71).

14.5.1.5. Simulations
The exposure metrics (AUCτ,ss, Cmax,ss, and Ctrough,ss) of donidalorsen and PD response following
80 mg Q4W, every month (Q1M), Q8W, or every 2 months (Q2M) were simulated based on the
final population PK/PD model and distribution of demographic data in subjects from Trials ISIS
721744-CS2 and ISIS 721744-CS5. The differences in median AUCτ,ss, Cmax,ss, and Ctrough,ss of
donidalorsen between the 80 mg Q4W and Q1M regimens and between the 80 mg Q8W and
Q2M regimens was <10% (Table 76 and Figure 72). The median PKK percent change from
baseline at the PK Ctrough,ss was similar for 80 mg Q1M compared to 80 mg Q4W (difference
<1%) and for 80 mg Q2M compared to 80 mg Q8W (difference <2%) (Figure 73).

15.1.1. Definition and Collection of HAE Attacks, Trial
CS5
During the trial, subjects were instructed to report details of any HAE attack to the trial site
within 72 hours of the onset of the attack. Throughout the Screening (Run-In Period), Treatment,
and Post-Treatment Periods, site personnel contacted the subjects approximately weekly, as well
as during trial visits, to inquire about attacks.
For each HAE attack, the following data were collected:


Date/time of symptom onset.



Location and description of symptoms:
– Peripheral angioedema: cutaneous swelling involving an extremity, face, neck, torso,
and/or genitourinary region.
– Abdominal angioedema: abdominal pain, with or without abdominal distension, nausea,
vomiting, or diarrhea.
– Laryngeal angioedema: stridor, dyspnea, difficulty speaking, difficulty swallowing, throat
tightening, or swelling of the tongue, palate, uvula, or larynx.



HAE attack severity:
– Mild: transient or mild discomfort.
– Moderate: mild to moderate limitation in activity, some assistance needed.
– Severe: marked limitation in activity, assistance required.



Need for assistance, medical intervention, emergency room (ER) visit, or hospitalization.



Medications to treat the attack.



HAE attack course, including if the HAE attack(s) in question was a typical attack for the
subject, or if there was an alternative diagnosis.



Date/time symptoms resolved.

The presence of these symptoms, including symptoms in one or more of the above locations, was
not necessarily considered an investigator-confirmed HAE attack (to be used in efficacy endpoint
analyses) unless the diagnosis was confirmed by the investigator. The investigator was permitted
to use clinical judgment regarding whether the symptoms represent a HAE attack or not. For
example, if the reported event was accompanied by symptoms not consistent with an HAE attack
(e.g., urticaria); if the reported event persisted well beyond the typical course of time for an HAE
attack (e.g., greater than 7 days); or if there was a likely alternative etiology for the event (e.g.,
viral gastroenteritis).
An HAE attack was defined as an event with signs or symptoms consistent with an attack in at
least one of the locations noted above. A discrete attack was counted if there was at least a 24hour symptom-free period between attacks. If there was less than 24 hours between the stop

232
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5646426

NDA 219407
Dawnzera (donidalorsen)
date/time of the first event and the start date/time of the next event, the events were combined
and counted as one unique attack.

15.1.2. Data and Safety Monitoring Committee, Trial
CS5
A Data and Safety Monitoring Committee was assembled to review safety and tolerability data
collected during this trial.

15.1.3. Sample Size Considerations, Trial CS5
The power and sample size estimations were calculated by the Applicant using simulations based
on a generalized linear model for count data assuming a Poisson distribution. The primary
endpoint was the time-normalized number of investigator-confirmed HAE attacks (per 4 weeks)
from Week 1 to Week 25. Assuming an HAE attack rate of 13.26 attacks per 6-month period in
the placebo group and an HAE attack rate of 1.38 attacks per 6-month period in the
donidalorsen-4 group, the sample size of 54 subjects (2:1 ratio) would provide at least 90%
power for the primary endpoint, with a 0.05 significance level. A total of approximately 84
subjects (42 in the donidalorsen-4 group, 21 in the placebo group, and 21 in the donidalorsen-8
group) were planned to be enrolled in this trial to account for potential early dropouts and to
facilitate some general safety evaluations.

protocol in the first amendment are summarized in Table 77 below. There were no substantial
changes made for the second amendment (dated July 12, 2022). The substantial changes in the
first amendment were reviewed by the Agency and deemed acceptable prior to trial subject
enrollment, which began in 2022.

15.1.5. Safety Assessments, Trial CS5
The safety and tolerability assessments included AEs, clinical laboratory parameters (chemistry,
coagulation, hematology, and urinalysis), vital signs, physical examinations, and ECG testing
according to the Schedule of Assessments (see Table 78). During the Treatment Period, these
assessments were generally collected every 4 weeks. A centralized laboratory was used to
enhance data quality.
For this trial, the adverse events of special interest were defined as platelet count <50,000/mm3
accompanied by a major bleeding event or clinically relevant non-major bleeding event, or
platelet count <25,000/mm3, independent of a major bleeding or clinically relevant non-major
bleeding event.
Overall, the safety assessments in Trial CS5 were adequate to inform the safety profile of
donidalorsen for the proposed use.

therapy. No drug-drug interaction with donidalorsen and the prior therapies were anticipated.

15.2.1.1. Sample Size Assumptions, Trial CS7
This was an uncontrolled, open-label trial not designed for statistical testing of a hypothesis, but
rather for long-term observation of safety and efficacy. The sample size for Trial CS7 was based
on the number of subjects enrolled in Trial CS5 and their eligibility to enroll in the open-label
extension trial. Eighty-three out of the 90 subjects in Trial CS5 enrolled as Rollover subjects in
Trial CS7. For Naïve subjects, sample size was selected based on clinical assessment. A total of
65 Naïve subjects enrolled in Trial CS7.

15.2.3. Primary, Secondary, and Exploratory
Objectives and Endpoints, Trial CS7
The primary objective of this trial was to evaluate the long-term safety of donidalorsen as
prophylaxis in patients with HAE. The primary endpoint was the incidence and severity of
TEAEs.
The secondary objectives of this trial were to evaluate the long-term efficacy and the effects of
donidalorsen on the number of HAE attacks and their impact on the QoL of patients with HAE.
The secondary endpoints were:


The time-normalized number of investigator-confirmed HAE attacks (per 4 weeks) from
Week 1 to Week 53.



The time-normalized number of investigator-confirmed HAE attacks (per 4 weeks) from
Week 5 to Week 53.



The percentage of investigator-confirmed HAE attack-free subjects from Week 5 to
Week 53.



The time-normalized number of moderate or severe investigator-confirmed HAE attacks (per
4 weeks) from Week 5 to Week 53.



The number of investigator-confirmed HAE attacks (per 4 weeks) requiring acute HAE
therapy from Week 5 to Week 53.



The Angioedema Quality of Life questionnaire total score over 52 weeks.

The exploratory objectives of this trial were to characterize the effects of donidalorsen on HAE
attacks, additional PROs, and biomarkers. The exploratory endpoints were:


All subjects:
– The time-normalized number of investigator-confirmed HAE attacks (per 4 weeks) from
Week 1 to Week 157.
– The Angioedema Quality of Life questionnaire total score over 157 weeks.
– Percentage of total days during the Treatment Period that subjects were attack free.
– Percentage of total months during the Treatment Period that subjects were attack free.
– Duration in days of the longest attack-free interval.
– Percent of subjects who were attack free for 6 or 12 consecutive months.
– Mean/median longest attack-free interval.
– Rate of HAE attacks that involve the larynx.
– Plasma PKK levels over 52 weeks.
– AECT over 52 weeks.
– Hereditary Angioedema Quality of Life questionnaire total score over 52 weeks.

15.3. Trial CS2
15.3.1. Trial Design, Trial CS2
Results from Trial CS2 support the efficacy and safety of donidalorsen for HAE attack
prevention. This was a two-part, phase 2, multicenter trial. Subjects were allocated into Part A or
Part B according to type of HAE, with either type I or II in Part A and type III in Part B. Parts A
and B were conducted concurrently. The trial visit schedule and procedures were nearly identical
in Parts A and B. Part B enrolled three adults with HAE type III for open-label treatment with
donidalorsen-4. Because Part B was uncontrolled and had a small sample size, it is not
considered adequate and well-controlled, and does not support efficacy or safety; the Agency’s
review focuses on Part A of Trial CS2 only.
Part A was a randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in 20 adults with HAE type I or
II in a 2:1 ratio to donidalorsen 80 mg (n=14) or placebo (n=6) SC every 4 weeks. The trial
schedule included a Screening Period of up to 8 weeks, a 12-week Treatment Period when
subjects received treatment every 4 weeks during 4 on-site trial visits, and a 4- to 13-week PostTreatment Period, with the duration determined by whether a subject enrolled in Trial CS3, the
follow-on OLE trial. Subjects completed post-treatment follow-up visits at Weeks 17, 21, and
26/Early Termination. Alternatively, subjects who completed the Week 17 trial visit and met
eligibility requirements started the Treatment Period in Trial CS3 any time after the Week 17
visit and discontinued participation in the Trial CS2 Post-Treatment Period. For subjects not
enrolling in the OLE trial, the final trial visit was the Week 26/Early Termination Visit. The trial
design is shown in Figure 75.
The length of trial participation for each subject was up to 8 months. Written and signed
informed consent was obtained prior to performance of any trial-related procedures, including
Screening. Each enrolled subject was randomized to begin trial treatment as soon as the subject
experienced ≥2 HAE attacks during the Screening Period.

15.3.3. Primary, Secondary, and Exploratory
Objectives and Endpoints, Trial CS2
The primary objective of Trial CS2 Part A was to evaluate the clinical efficacy of donidalorsen
in patients with HAE types I and II. The primary endpoint was the time-normalized number of
HAE attacks (per month) from Week 1 to Week 17. HAE attack information was collected as
described in Section 15.1.1. An HAE attack was defined as an event with signs or symptoms
consistent with an attack in at least one of the following locations: peripheral, abdominal, or
laryngeal. A discrete attack was counted if there was at least a 24-hour symptom-free period
between attacks. This definition of HAE attacks is subtly different than the investigatorconfirmed definition used in the phase 3 trials, but not expected to impact the Agency’s overall
conclusions, as this trial was intended to provide proof-of-concept and not SEE.
The secondary objectives of Trial CS2 Part A were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of
donidalorsen in patients with HAE types I and II and to evaluate the effects of donidalorsen on
plasma PKK and other biomarkers. The secondary endpoints, which were not tested with Type I
error control, included:


The time-normalized number of HAE attacks (per month) from Week 5 to Week 17.



The time-normalized number of moderate or severe HAE attacks (per month) from Week 5
to Week 17.



The number of subjects with a clinical response (defined as a ≥50%, ≥70%, or ≥90%
reduction from Baseline in HAE attack rate) by Week 17.



The number of HAE attacks requiring acute therapy from Week 5 to Week 17.



Cleaved high molecular weight kininogen (cHK) levels at Weeks 9 and 17.



Prekallikrein activity at Weeks 9 and 17.



Consumption of on-demand medication at Weeks 9 and 17.



Angioedema Quality of Life questionnaire score at Weeks 9 and 17.

The exploratory objectives were to evaluate PK over time and assess potential PK/PD
correlations on biomarkers and clinical outcomes. The exploratory endpoints included:


The number of HAE attack-free subjects by Week 17.



Pharmacokinetic parameters, including, but not limited to: Cmax, Tmax, AUC, and half-life
(t½).



Potential exposure response analysis using relevant exposure parameters and biomarkers.
